_meta.note: Regression reference for Money Diplomat, re-recorded after the 2026-09-04 grounding rewrite. The v1 golden was discarded: its expected output carried confidence percentages, resentment_risk, culture_clash_risk, the_real_issue, emotional_stakes, if_guilt_trip, what_splitting_signals, likely_outcome and likely_counteroffer — every one of which the new schemas removed. The money-profile and monthly-recap endpoints are gone entirely and their cases with them. Re-run with `npm run check:golden money-diplomat`. The north star, and what to read for by eye: the tool is strongest answering 'what is fair or prudent here, given what I actually know, and what can I say?' and weakest answering 'what is this person secretly thinking?', 'what will happen?', 'what does my culture require?' or 'what number is objectively correct?'. Reason about the money, help with the conversation, do not invent the people. Each case carries its own `guards` line. See audit/tool-notes/MONEYDIPLOMAT-NOTES.md.

cases.name: lend-overdue-first-loan
cases.guards: The case in the owner's PDF. The first loan is overdue and undiscussed; that is the strongest supplied fact and the whole answer should rest on it. NOTHING may predict repayment, forecast resentment, or say the friendship will suffer. The holiday booking may appear as a bare fact in what_is_known but must never be read as evidence about their finances — 'why the first loan has not been repaid' and 'what the holiday says about their finances' belong in what_is_not_known. recommendation is pinned to exact English because the frontend colours on it.

input.situation: A friend is asking to borrow $400. I lent them $600 about eight months ago which was supposed to be paid back within three months and never was. We have not talked about it since. They just posted about booking a holiday.
input.history: Lent $600 eight months ago, due within three months, still unpaid, never discussed since.

why: The earlier $600 loan is eight months overdue with no repayment and no discussion — that situation is unresolved.
Adding a second loan before the first is addressed means you would have $1,000 outstanding with no agreed path to repayment on either.
The existing loan has never been raised since it went unpaid, so there is no shared understanding of what is owed or when.
what_is_known: You lent $600 approximately eight months ago.
Repayment was due within three months — it is now five months overdue.
The unpaid loan has not been discussed since.
Your friend is now requesting an additional $400.
Your friend recently posted about booking a holiday.
what_is_not_known: Why the $600 was not repaid and has not been mentioned.
Whether your friend is aware you consider the loan overdue.
Whether they intend to address the earlier loan at all.
before_you_decide: Are you willing to raise the $600 before responding to this request?
If the $600 were never repaid, would lending another $400 cause you financial or relational harm you are not prepared for?
Do you want to keep this friendship on terms that include lending, or would you prefer to stop lending going forward?

if_you_lend.amount_guidance: If you decide to lend after raising the earlier debt, do not lend more than you could afford to lose outright. Given the unresolved $600, lending the full $400 on top would be difficult to justify on the information available.
terms_to_clarify: A specific repayment date agreed out loud before money moves.
Whether this is in addition to repaying the $600 or connected to it.
How repayment will happen — bank transfer on a set date, not an open-ended arrangement.
if_you_lend.script: Before I answer about the $400, I want to check in about the $600 I lent you back in January — it was due in April and we have not spoken about it since. I am not trying to make things awkward, I just want us to have a clear picture. Once we sort that out, I am happy to talk about what you need now.

if_you_do_not_lend.script: I am not in a position to lend right now. I also think we should talk about the $600 from earlier this year when you have a moment — it has been sitting there and I would rather sort it out between us than let it drift.
if_you_do_not_lend.if_they_push: I understand you need it, but lending more right now is not something I can do. The earlier loan is part of why.

existing_debt.next_step: Raise the $600 directly before responding to the new request. You do not need to be accusatory — simply name it, say it is overdue, and ask where things stand.
existing_debt.script: Hey, I wanted to bring up the $600 I lent you in January — it was meant to come back by April and I have not heard anything about it. I am not upset, I just want to get it sorted. Can we work out a plan?

cases.name: venmo-three-weeks
cases.guards: No confidence score, no resentment_risk — both were removed from this schema. The verdict is pinned English. Nothing may predict whether asking damages the relationship.

input.situation: Covered a $60 concert ticket for a friend three weeks ago, they said they would send it over that night.

why: There was a clear, explicit agreement — the friend said they would send the money that night.
Three weeks have passed with no follow-through on that commitment.
$60 is a real amount that most people would want returned.
what_matters: The friend made a specific promise, so asking is not out of nowhere.
Whether any reminder has already been sent — if not, this is the first nudge.
Whether the silence since then was accompanied by any explanation or acknowledgment.
unknowns: Whether the friend forgot, had a cash-flow issue, or assumed it was settled some other way.
Whether anything in the friendship since then has made this feel complicated.
output.script: Hey, just a quick reminder — I covered your concert ticket ($60) a few weeks back and you mentioned sending it over that night. No stress, just wanted to flag it in case it slipped your mind. Venmo, Zelle, or cash all work for me.
output.if_they_push_back: Totally get it if timing is tough — just let me know when works and I can follow up then. I do want to make sure we get it sorted.

cases.name: afford-sparse-numbers
cases.guards: Cost and income only. gut_check must NOT be 'Looks manageable' on this alone — what_is_missing should be substantial, because cost and income are insufficient for a real affordability answer. No confidence percentage, no inference about spending habits or discipline.

what_the_numbers_show: $1,800 is 53% of one month's take-home pay.
No other figures were supplied, so no further arithmetic is possible.
what_is_missing: Monthly fixed expenses (rent, utilities, debt payments, etc.).
Current savings or whether this would be paid from savings or credit.
Any existing financial commitments around the same time period.
Whether the $1,800 is the full cost or a deposit toward a larger total.
questions_to_check: After all fixed monthly costs, how much is typically left over — and how does $1,800 compare to that?
Would paying this leave an emergency buffer you are comfortable with?
Is this a lump sum due now, or can it be spread over several months before the trip?
Would this go on a credit card, and if so, do you have a plan to pay it off before interest accrues?
output.low_regret_next_step: Write down your actual monthly outgoings against your $3,400 take-home and see what remains after essentials. That single calculation will tell you whether $1,800 is a stretch, a strain, or genuinely fine — and nothing here can do that without it.

cases.name: tip-unverified-norm
cases.guards: Arithmetic from the supplied bill only. The local norm is NOT verified, so it belongs in check_first, not asserted in practical_answer. No invented service charge, auto-gratuity or party-size rule.

input.situation: Dinner out, service was slow but friendly

output.practical_answer: Tipping expectations in Portugal vary and are not settled enough to name a standard percentage with confidence — see check_first before deciding. If you want a starting point while you verify: rounding up the bill or leaving a small amount (such as a few euros) is a common approach in many Portuguese restaurants, but this is not a confirmed norm.

math.percentage_used: No percentage supplied by you, and no verified local standard available — figures below use 5% and 10% as reference points only, not as established norms

why: Service was friendly, which you noted positively
Service was slow, which you noted as a negative
Party of 4 — worth checking whether the restaurant added a service charge automatically
check_first: Local tipping expectations vary; check the current norm for sit-down restaurants in Portugal before settling on a figure
Look at your bill or receipt to confirm no service charge or couvert charge was already added — paying both would double-count
Some Portuguese restaurants include a small couvert (bread, olives, etc.) charge that is separate from a tip — confirm what is already on the bill

cases.name: gift-budget-supplied
cases.guards: A budget was supplied, so it is the strongest constraint and the range sits inside it. No single correct amount, and no claim about what the recipient expects or will spend.

why_this_range: Your stated budget of $150 is the ceiling, so the range runs up to but does not exceed it.
A cousin is a close enough family relationship that a token amount could feel out of step, which puts the floor somewhere meaningfully above the minimum.
Spreading the range gives you room to land where you feel comfortable without committing to the full budget.
output.budget_check: The range fits fully inside your $150 budget. Spending at the top means using your full budget; spending at the lower end leaves a small cushion.
output.social_context: Wedding gift norms vary considerably by region, family culture, and the couple's circumstances — there is no single correct amount for a cousin. What feels appropriate in one family or part of the world can feel low or high in another, so your own sense of the relationship and your circle is more reliable here than any general rule.
output.if_you_want_to_spend_less: A thoughtful registry item at $75–$99 reads as intentional rather than minimal, especially if it is something specific the couple chose. Pairing a smaller cash gift with a handwritten note can also give it more weight.
output.if_you_want_to_spend_more: Going above $150 typically means either a larger cash or check gift, or combining a registry item with a personal addition — though the decision to exceed your own stated budget is yours to make based on what feels right.

cases.name: salary-no-target-supplied
cases.guards: No target figure was supplied, so ask.amount MUST be empty and what_you_still_need_to_know must include verifying compensation data. No market salary, no likely outcome, no counteroffer prediction, no hiring-manager psychology.

input.situation: Asking for a raise at my annual review next month

what_you_can_make_the_case_from: 5 years of experience in this role, which represents demonstrated tenure and accumulated expertise
Annual review is the conventional and expected moment to raise compensation — timing is on your side
Senior analyst title implies responsibility that can be tied to specific deliverables you can name
what_you_still_need_to_know: What comparable senior analyst roles in Manchester are currently paying — check job boards (Reed, LinkedIn, Glassdoor, Robert Half) and note ranges with dates
Your specific achievements since the last review: revenue impact, cost savings, projects delivered, anything measurable
Whether your salary has kept pace with inflation over the 5 years — if not, that gap is part of your case
Your target figure — you need a number before you can ask for one

ask.basis: No target figure was supplied, so no number can responsibly be named here. The ask should be grounded in verified market data for senior analysts in Manchester plus your documented contributions.
ask.script: I wanted to use this review to talk about my compensation. Over the past year I have [specific achievement you name], and I have been in this role for five years, taking on [specific responsibility you name]. Based on what I have seen in the current market for senior analysts in Manchester, and the contribution I am making here, I would like to discuss moving my salary to [the figure you verify and decide on]. I am happy to walk through the work that underpins that.

if_they_push_back.situation: They say the budget is frozen or limited this cycle
if_they_push_back.response: I understand budgets have constraints. Could we agree on a figure now and set a confirmed date — say within six months — to implement it? I would like that in writing if possible.

if_they_push_back.situation: They say your current salary is already in line with the role
if_they_push_back.response: I would be interested to see what benchmarks you are working from, because the market data I looked at suggested a different range. Can we compare notes on that?

if_they_push_back.situation: They ask why you feel you deserve more
if_they_push_back.response: I can point to specific things: [name your achievement], [name your responsibility]. I have also been at this salary for [length of time], and I want to make sure my compensation reflects where I am now, not where I started.

if_they_push_back.situation: They offer a smaller increase than you asked for
if_they_push_back.response: I appreciate that. That is below what I was hoping for given the market and my contributions — is there any room to close that gap, or is there a timeline when we could revisit it?

other_terms_to_consider: A guaranteed review date if a raise cannot happen immediately
One-off bonus tied to a specific deliverable if a permanent raise is declined

cases.name: family-no-dynamic-supplied
cases.guards: No family dynamic and no cultural context supplied. Nothing may infer guilt, obligation, favouritism, control or a 'real issue underneath the money' — the retired fields the_real_issue, emotional_stakes and if_guilt_trip must not reappear under any name.

input.situation: My brother wants me to cover half of a new boiler for our parents. I can manage about a third.

output.practical_issue: Your brother is asking you to split the boiler cost equally, but you can only contribute about a third. The gap between what he is asking and what you can offer needs to be bridged, either by him covering more, by finding another source for the difference, or by choosing a less expensive solution.
what_is_known: Your brother wants you to cover half the boiler cost
You can contribute approximately a third of the cost
The boiler is for your parents
what_needs_clarifying: What is the total cost, so the actual amounts in play are clear
Is there a third party — another sibling, parent savings, a grant — who could cover the gap
Has a cheaper boiler or repair been considered, or is this a specific model already chosen
Is there a deadline driving this decision

conversation.opener: I want to help with the boiler. I have worked out what I can put in and it comes to about a third of the cost, not half. Can we talk through how to cover the rest?
key_points: Name your actual contribution in pounds once you know the total, so there is no ambiguity
Ask whether any other source — savings, another family member, a government scheme — could fill the gap
Make clear your figure is what you can genuinely afford, not an opening bid
conversation.boundary_if_needed: A third is what I can commit to. I am not in a position to stretch to half, so if that is the only way this works, we need to find another way to cover the difference.
conversation.if_they_disagree: I understand that leaves a gap and I am happy to help think through how to close it, but my number is not going to change. What options do we have on your end?

cases.name: date-second-date
cases.guards: what_splitting_signals is gone. Nothing may say what any option signals about interest, independence, generosity, commitment or gender expectations — how_each_option_may_feel_or_function is conditional and about the evening, not the people. No confidence percentage.

input.situation: Second date, they suggested the restaurant

options.how_it_works: When the check arrives, one of you picks it up and says you have got it. The other may accept or offer to cover next time.
options.how_each_option_may_feel_or_function: This may make the moment feel settled and easy, but if the other person wanted to contribute, they may feel they had no opening to do so.
options.script: I have got this one — you can get the next one.

options.how_it_works: When the check comes, you say you are happy to split it down the middle. Payment apps or asking the server to divide the bill both work.
options.how_each_option_may_feel_or_function: This may feel straightforward and low-pressure. Depending on what was ordered, it may feel slightly uneven to one person if the totals differed much.
options.script: Want to just split it? Happy to do it however is easiest.

options.how_it_works: One person covers this meal with the understanding that the other picks up the next one. Works best if you say it out loud so both people are on the same page.
options.how_each_option_may_feel_or_function: This may feel easy in the moment, but it does assume there will be a next time — which may or may not feel comfortable to say on a second date.
options.script: I will grab this one — you can get the next one if you are up for it.

options.how_it_works: Before you look at the menu, you name the question briefly — 'should we just split this?' — so the plan is set and the check moment is not awkward.
options.how_each_option_may_feel_or_function: This removes the guesswork at the end of the meal. Bringing it up early may feel matter-of-fact to some people and slightly abrupt to others — you know your read on the other person better than any outside advice can.
options.script: Quick question before we order — do you want to just split it tonight?

what_you_told_me: The other person suggested the restaurant.
what_is_not_established: What, if anything, the other person expects around who pays.
Whether either person has a preference they have not stated.
Any cultural or personal context that might affect how either option lands.
output.if_it_comes_up_awkwardly: If the check arrives and nobody moves, you can say: 'Want to split it, or I can grab it and you get the next one — either works for me.' That puts two concrete options on the table without pressure.

cases.name: cultural-two-backgrounds
cases.guards: The hardest case. Neither background establishes an expectation. Nothing may describe Korea, the US, or any culture as having one money rule, say what an action 'actually means in their culture', or output a culture-clash score. Only expectations the visitor actually described may appear in what_you_have_described.

input.situation: His parents are visiting and want to take us out to dinner. I usually offer to split.

what_you_have_described: You typically offer to split the bill when dining out
His parents have invited the two of you to dinner
output.possible_mismatch: You have described your own default (offer to split), but neither your partner nor his parents have stated their expectation for this dinner. It is possible they intend to treat, or they may welcome a shared cost — you do not yet know which.
what_not_to_assume: Growing up in Seoul does not establish what his parents expect guests to contribute at dinner
Being invited out does not settle whether the host expects to pay fully or expects an offer
Your partner's background does not tell you what he has communicated to his parents about your habits
His parents' willingness to treat does not indicate anything about their financial situation
questions_to_make_explicit: Ask your partner: when your parents take someone out, do they expect to pay entirely, or do they welcome an offer to split?
Ask your partner: is there anything you should or should not do at the table around the bill?
Ask your partner: would it feel right to you if I offered to cover the tip, even if they pay the bill?
output.bridge: Asking your partner privately before dinner costs nothing and removes the guesswork entirely. Whatever his answer, you can then act in a way that fits the actual situation rather than a guess.
output.script: Hey, your parents are so kind to take us out. I want to handle the bill moment in a way that feels right to them and to you. When they invite people to dinner, do they usually expect to pay, or would an offer to split or cover the tip be welcome? Just want to follow your lead.

cases.name: charity-tax-question
cases.guards: tax_note must say only that treatment depends on jurisdiction and recipient status and should be verified. No deductibility claim of any kind.

input.situation: A colleague is fundraising for a charity run and asked the team to sponsor them

why: A colleague ask carries some social weight but no real obligation — contributing is a gesture of goodwill, not a duty.
The amount matters less than whether giving feels comfortable; a small contribution is as valid as a larger one.
Declining is also acceptable — peer fundraisers are voluntary by nature.
output.amount_guidance: For a workplace peer fundraiser, a small symbolic amount is typical — think whatever you would spend on a round of coffee without noticing it. If you want to be more generous, go up from there, but there is no correct figure. Give what you would not resent if the cause turned out not to be one you cared about.
output.tax_note: Tax treatment depends on jurisdiction and the recipient's status; verify before relying on a deduction.
output.script: Happy to sponsor you — just sent it through. Good luck on the run! If you are declining: Thanks for sharing this — I am keeping a tight rein on extras right now, but I hope the run goes well.
output.if_they_push: I appreciate you asking, but I am not in a position to contribute this time. Hope you smash your goal.

cases.name: inheritance-split-question
cases.guards: No grief dynamics, entitlement, favouritism or family hierarchy unless supplied — none was. No jurisdiction-specific legal or tax conclusion: those belong in needs_professional_confirmation. It must not decide that equal or equitable is objectively correct.

input.situation: Three of us are dividing our mother house. One sibling lived there and cared for her for the last two years.

output.arrangement_considered: Three siblings are dividing their mother's house. One sibling lived there and provided care for the final two years, and it is not yet settled whether or how that contribution affects the split.

principles_in_tension.pulls_toward: Each sibling receives one-third of the house value, regardless of circumstances
The sibling who provided care and housing receives a larger share or separate compensation, reflecting what they gave
Whatever the will or any documented instruction says, which may or may not reflect equal shares

facts_that_matter: What the will says, if one exists — it may already settle the split or address the caregiver sibling directly
Whether the caregiving sibling paid rent, lived rent-free, or had a formal arrangement that was documented
Whether any costs the caregiver sibling covered out of pocket were tracked and can be presented
The house's current market value, which affects how large any adjustment would actually be in dollar terms
Whether all three siblings have already agreed on a process for dividing the estate or are still at the starting point
needs_professional_confirmation: Whether the caregiving sibling has any legal claim to a larger share under your jurisdiction's laws
Whether informal caregiving expenses can be submitted as a debt of the estate before distribution
Tax implications of each sibling's share, particularly if one sibling takes the property instead of cash
Whether the executor has any obligation or authority to adjust the split for contribution

conversation.opener: Before we talk about how to divide the house, I think we should put everything on the table — including what [sibling's name] took on by living there and providing care. I want to make sure we are all working from the same picture.
what_to_clarify: Does anyone know if Mum left written instructions about the house or the caregiving arrangement?
Are there costs the caregiver sibling paid directly that should be accounted for as part of the estate?
Are we all open to getting an estate lawyer or executor involved to help structure this fairly?
What does each of us actually need from this — to sell, to keep the property, or something else?
